short: Armigeri (latin) translates as «armored, equipped for war», but has a much broader definition. The word itself comes from arma «military equipment» plus gerere «to carry» and literally translates as Armadillos or much more understandable meaning Squires, but to compare them, exactly with the squires of the Middle Ages, is not worth it at all, because even in late medieval England this word referred not to a simple squire, accompanying the knight, but a special one - carrying his own distinctive emblem. Armigeri should probably be meant as «armored» or even «heavily armored». Many historians believe that armigeri cavalry units were the equivalent of cataphracts. It is quite possible that the soldiers of these legions were particularly well protected or armed; another explanation may be that they earned this nickname or insignia by showing themselves by their fortitude. The word «armaturarum» has a very similar meaning to armigeri. Equites - a new type of cavalry appeared in the 3rd century (probably under Diocletian), has nothing in common with the ancient Roman class of Equites (cavalrymen) or legionary cavalry of the Principate period (equites legionis). Literally translated from Latin as «horsemen», it is a cavalry unit of any type.
history: Since Rome's beginnings, as was common in almost all ancient societies, the noble class were the only people who could afford horses, and were therefore most likely to own one. As a result, early Roman armies fielded cavalry consisting entirely of nobles - the equestrian class - and then bolstered their comparatively small numbers with units formed from the city's Italian Socii allies. Due to a number of high profile defeats, such as their poor showing during Hannibal's climactic Italian campaign at the end of the 3rd century BC, Roman cavalry contingents were generally considered to be far weaker than their Italian counterparts whilst purely a unit of nobles. Eventually the Socii were granted Roman citizenship and, following a number of reforms to the army's structure, were folded into its ranks. Wherever the Romans went after that they drew on local specialists to swell their numbers as auxiliary troops. By the time of the Hunnic incursions, auxiliaries had been made a part of the Legions, resulting in Rome being able to field some of the best, most adaptable cavalry in the ancient world.
strengths: Very low damage and armour penetration
